title: Volume 9 · Permissions, Workflows and Automation
subtitle: Lessons 5–8: roles that match the org chart, restrictions that hold, a discount workflow, and automation that does not run away
outcomes: Build roles and permissions that match who does what
Restrict a user to their own warehouse or branch without custom code
Add an approval workflow for discounts and prove it blocks what it should
Automate recurring documents safely and know what to leave manual

slides.title: Roles that match the org chart, not the software
bullets: A role is a job function, so name it after the job and not after a person
Permission levels control what can be created, read, amended or deleted
Start restrictive and add, because removing access later is a political fight
Every role needs an owner who reviews membership quarterly

rows: Read, Write, Create, Submit; no Delete or Cancel
Create and submit buttons present, delete absent

slides.notes: The instinct is to grant everything because the demo is easier, and the consequence arrives six months later when a salesperson deletes a submitted order. Start with read, write, create and submit; add cancel only for supervisors, and delete for nobody in a transaction doctype. A functional consultant who can explain that sentence has already delivered value.

slides.title: Restrict a user to their own warehouse
bullets: User permissions filter the data a role can see, and they outweigh role permissions
A warehouse restriction is the standard way to keep branches apart without separate companies
Test as the restricted user, because administrators bypass these filters
Restrictions apply to reports too, which is what makes them trustworthy
slides.notes: This is the single most requested control in multi-branch distribution, and it is pure configuration. Show the client the same report from two logins, because seeing the difference is what sells the control. Remind them that administrators bypass it, so the discipline depends on limiting administrator accounts to two named people.

slides.title: Put an approval on discounts above ten per cent
bullets: A workflow adds states and allowed transitions, so a document cannot jump to submitted
Conditions belong in transition rules, which keeps the workflow honest
Approvers need a role, not a person, so absence does not block the business
Every workflow needs an escape path, or urgent orders stall at month end

rows: Draft to Approved when discount is zero
Draft to Pending Approval when discount above 10
One order at 5 per cent, one at 15 per cent

slides.notes: The workflow is only useful if the client's approver role is filled by more than one person, so ask that question before building it. A fifteen per cent discount order that sits unapproved for three days costs more than the discount saved. Build the escape path deliberately and document who may use it.

slides.title: Automate recurring documents, carefully
bullets: Auto repeat creates a copy of a document on a schedule, which suits subscriptions and retainers
Test one cycle before enabling, because a wrong template repeats the error monthly
Automation never replaces the control, so someone still reviews the output
Start with one low-risk document and add others only after a clean month

rows: Sales Invoice for the monthly retainer

slides.notes: Automation is where a small configuration error compounds twelve times a year, so the first cycle must be reviewed by a person. A retainer invoice that repeats the wrong tax template creates a filing problem every month. Enable one document, watch one cycle, then expand, and write that rule into the handover note.

slides.title: Same report, two logins
bullets: The test is not what the administrator sees but what the restricted role sees
Reports, lists and link fields must all respect the filter, not only forms
A restriction that silently does not apply is worse than no restriction at all
Record the test result, because the client will ask for evidence

rows: New stock entry as that user
screenshot or note in the handover file

slides.notes: Two logins, one report, a visible difference: that is the demonstration clients remember. Write the result down, because when the first complaint arrives about missing data the answer is already documented. If both logins look identical, the user permission was saved against the wrong field.

slides.title: States, roles and the escape path
bullets: A workflow is correct when a low-discount order flows and a high-discount order waits
Approvers must see the document in their queue, not hunt for it by number
The escape path is documented and named, so emergencies do not become policy
Rejection is a state, not a deletion, so the history survives

rows: status Rejected, retained in the list
Sales Order list filtered by state
Workflow notes in the handover file

slides.notes: The failure mode is a workflow with no queue, where the approver only learns about the order when the customer calls. Configure the queue view as part of the build, not afterwards, and teach the approver to work from it. A rejection that deletes the document would destroy the audit trail, which is why the state is retained.

slides.title: Automation options ranked by risk
bullets: Permissions are the highest-value change and the lowest risk, so start there
Notifications are cheap and reversible; workflows change behaviour and need agreement
Auto repeat touches money documents, so it needs the tightest review
Every option here is configuration, and every one needs an owner

rows: Named approver role and escape path

slides.notes: Ranking by risk is what stops a client asking for everything at once. Permissions first, notifications second, workflow once the approver role exists, and auto repeat only for documents that are genuinely identical every period. Say the order out loud in the proposal and the delivery becomes predictable.

slides.title: The access review a consultant should leave behind
bullets: Access reviews are a quarterly ritual, not a one-off configuration task
List every user, their roles and any user permissions, and get a signature
Remove leavers on the day they leave, which is the only control auditors test hard
Keep two administrators, named, and no shared logins

rows: each has a user permission row

slides.notes: This sheet takes twenty minutes a quarter and prevents the finding that audits always produce: a leaver with live access. Hand it to the client as a template rather than a lecture, and put the first review date in the handover document. Consulting value often looks like a checklist somebody actually uses.

lab.title: Lab · Roles, a warehouse restriction, a discount workflow and an auto repeat
steps: Create the Sales Executive role with read, write, create and submit but no delete
Restrict a warehouse supervisor to Retail Counter with a user permission
Log in as that user and confirm only their warehouse appears in reports
Build a sales order workflow with an approval state above 10 per cent discount
Test a 5 per cent order and confirm it submits without approval
Test a 15 per cent order and confirm it waits in Pending Approval
Set an auto repeat for a monthly retainer invoice
Review the first generated draft and confirm amounts and tax
lab.done: Done when the restricted user sees one warehouse only, the 15 per cent order cannot submit without approval, and the auto repeat produced a correct draft for review.

quiz.question: Which permission should a sales role normally lack on submitted documents?
quiz.why: Delete on transaction doctypes destroys the audit trail. Sales roles normally read, create, write and submit, with cancel reserved for supervisors.

quiz.question: What does a user permission do?
options: Filters the records a user can see
quiz.why: User permissions restrict data, such as one warehouse or territory, and they apply to reports as well as forms.

quiz.question: Why should an approver be a role rather than a named person?
options: So the process continues when someone is away
quiz.why: A role keeps the workflow moving during leave, whereas a named approver blocks the business whenever they are unavailable.

quiz.question: What is the main risk of auto repeat?
quiz.why: Auto repeat copies a document on a schedule, so a wrong tax template or price repeats monthly until somebody reviews the draft.

quiz.question: Which automation should a consultant configure first?
quiz.why: Permissions deliver the highest control value with the lowest risk and are fully reversible, which is why they come first.

memory.spine: A role says what a job may do, a user permission says which rows it may see, and the only test that counts is the restricted login.

device.label: Roles do, permissions see
expansion: Name roles after the job function, never after a person
User permissions filter rows and outweigh what the role would otherwise show
A workflow adds states and allowed transitions, so a document cannot jump to submitted
Auto repeat copies a document on a schedule, which suits subscriptions and retainers only
Test the restricted login, not the administrator

cards.q: Role permission or user permission, what is the difference?
cards.a: A role grants actions on a DocType, a user permission filters the records, and the narrower wins.

cards.q: How is a user kept to one warehouse?
cards.a: With a user permission on Warehouse for that user, not with a new role.

cards.q: What makes a discount workflow correct?
cards.a: A low discount flows straight to submitted while a high one waits at pending approval for the right role.
For genuinely recurring documents with a fixed shape, never for ones a human must judge.

cards.q: What does an access review check?
cards.a: That every active login still matches a job, quarterly, including the ones nobody uses.

trap.what: A user permission is added to fix a report that looks wrong.
trap.why: The report was the symptom of an over broad role, so filtering rows hides the grant and the next report breaks differently.

narration: Permissions are the least glamorous part of a project and the part that determines whether it survives an audit. Roles follow the org chart, not the software, and the safe default is read, write, create and submit without delete. User permissions restrict a person to their warehouse or territory, and you prove it by logging in as them, because administrators bypass the filter. Then workflow: a discount above ten per cent waits for the sales manager, and the approver is a role so leave does not stop the business. Finally automation, where one wrong template repeats twelve times a year, so review the first cycle. Configure in that order and the client gets control before convenience, and finish with a quarterly access review that the client signs, because a leaver with live access is the finding every audit produces when nobody owns the list, and when nobody has written down who is allowed to do what.
